solutionSteps: \textnormal{Every factor is positive. Pair an even index with the following odd index and write u and v for their positive magnitudes.}

\textnormal{The sum of u minus v converges by the alternating test. For large k, the negative product term has size proportional to k to the power minus twice p and dominates u minus v whenever twice p is at most one.}
\textnormal{If p is at most one half, each paired logarithm is eventually negative and asymptotic to minus uv. Their sum diverges to minus infinity, and the product tends to zero.}
\textnormal{If p exceeds one half, expand each logarithm to first order. The remainders are absolutely summable because they are bounded by a constant times n to the power minus twice p.}
\textnormal{The logarithm sum then has a finite real limit, giving a strictly positive product. An unpaired final factor tends to one and does not change either conclusion.}

solutionSteps: \textnormal{Let }A_L\textnormal{ be the number of allowed positive integers with exactly L digits. The first digit is one, and the following digit, when present, must be zero. Splitting the remaining strings by their final digit gives the Fibonacci recurrence.}

\textnormal{For a positive exponent p, every integer in the L-digit block lies between the corresponding consecutive powers of the base. Its whole block contribution is therefore bounded above and below by fixed multiples of the same geometric scale.}

\textnormal{The growing characteristic root determines convergence. At equality the block contributions stay bounded away from zero, so the boundary diverges. For nonpositive p the summands themselves cannot tend to zero.}
